sections.title: Why 'Ways' and Not 'Matters': Bi'ah, Natural Course, or Distinction?
sections.gist: Continuing the question of why the Mishnah says a woman is acquired in three “ways”: explanations from *bi'ah* and from R. Shimon, a test against the *zav* and *etrog* mishnayot, and, once the *koy* and Gittin break the pattern, a formal rule.

children.title: Explained by the Topic: Bi'ah and R. Shimon's 'Way of a Man'
children.gist: Two explanations tie “ways” to the subject of *kiddushin*: all three modes serve *bi'ah*, or the Mishnah alludes to R. Shimon's teaching that it is the way of a man to pursue a woman.

children.title: Money and Document Too: All for the Sake of Bi'ah
children.gist: Granted that intercourse is called a “way”, why use the word for money and document? Because they too are for the sake of *bi'ah*.

bullets.text: Challenge: “way” suits intercourse, which is called a way, but for money and a document the Mishnah could have said “matters”.
Answer: since intercourse had to be listed, the Mishnah used “way” for all three.
Challenge: would the Mishnah phrase two cases to suit one? Answer: money and document are also for the sake of intercourse, since the marital relationship is the purpose of betrothal.
A parallel to *nikneit*: that term strictly fits only *kesef* yet frames the whole institution; “way” strictly fits only *bi'ah* yet frames all three modes.

Rashi cites his teachers (with the Geonim) that *kiddushei kesef* is rabbinic, and the Rambam calls it *mi'divrei soferim*. If *bi'ah* is the primary Torah mode, “for the sake of *bi'ah*” is a claim about how *kiddushin* is built, not just about wording.

The Rambam notes that before the Torah, marriage was made by *bi'ah* alone, the most natural of the modes. A participant suggested *bi'ah* is the primary act of *kiddushin* itself, with money and document serving that act.

children.title: R. Shimon: The Owner Searches for His Lost Object
children.gist: The Torah says “when a man takes a woman” because a man pursues a woman as the owner searches for his lost item: she was created from his side.

bullets.text: Alternatively, the Mishnah follows R. Shimon's *baraita*: why does the Torah say “when a man takes a woman” (Devarim 22:13), and not “when a woman is taken by a man”?
Because it is the way of a man to pursue a woman, and not the way of a woman to pursue a man.
Parable: a man who lost an item. The owner searches for his lost item, not the reverse. Since woman was created from man's side, he seeks what he lost.
The *aveidah* image still has a possessive note, but a lost part of oneself is not a commodity. It echoes “*ve'davak be'ishto ve'hayu le'vasar echad*”: two halves made whole again.

This recasts the man's active role: not because she is an object being bought, but because he has lost something and must search. The move is from domination to longing, and the *kinyan* and *bi'ah* models sit side by side.
The pattern of the man as initiator is still recognizable today, and it underlies the halakha that the man is the active party in the act of *kiddushin*.

children.title: Zav and Etrog: 'Way' as the Natural Course
children.gist: Other mishnayot also say “ways”, and the Gemara explains each by a natural course: eating and drinking lead to *zivah*, and the *etrog* grows and is tithed like a vegetable.

bullets.text: Challenge: “one examines a *zav* in seven ways”: why not “matters”? Answer: it teaches that excessive eating and excessive drinking are ways that lead to *zivah*.
Challenge: Bikkurim 2:6, “an *etrog* tree is like a tree in three ways”. Answer: because the latter clause says it is like a vegetable in one way.
But why “way” in the latter clause? Because the *etrog*'s way is like a vegetable's: it is watered by all water, not rain alone, and tithed according to when it is harvested.
So a vegetable, or an *etrog*, picked in a year of poor man's tithe gives that tithe, even if it budded in a year of second tithe.
On this reading “way” signals natural causation, how a body or a plant actually operates, and not an arbitrary list. Carried back to *kiddushin*, it points to *bi'ah* as the most natural mode.

Rashi: the *etrog*'s likeness to a tree includes *orlah* and *neta reva'i*; its likeness to a vegetable is that its *ma'aser* follows the time of picking, since it grows year-round and is not tied to one season.

children.title: The Koy and Gittin: No Natural Course to Explain
children.gist: Two more mishnayot say “ways” where no natural course is involved: the *koy*, and the ways bills of divorce resemble bills of manumission.

bullets.text: Challenge: Bikkurim 2:8 says the *koy* has ways like a wild animal, ways like a domesticated animal, ways like both and ways like neither. Why not “matters”?
And Gittin 9a: “this is one of the ways in which bills of divorce are like bills of manumission”. Why not “matters”?
Having invoked natural order, the Gemara brings hybrids, the *etrog* and the *koy*, as if showing how untidy natural order really is.

children.title: The Rule: 'Ways' Where There Is a Distinction, 'Matters' Where None
children.gist: The Gemara drops the topic-based explanations: “ways” marks a distinction between possibilities, “matters” a list with none, as R. Eliezer's “every matter” proves.

returns_to.note: Replaces the topic-based explanations of “ways” in our Mishnah

bullets.text: Rather, the wording does not depend on the topic. Wherever there is a distinction, the Mishnah says “ways”; where there is none, it says “matters”.
Proof from the same *etrog* Mishnah: R. Eliezer says the *etrog* tree is like a tree in every matter. With no distinction, it says “matter”. The Gemara concludes: learn from this.
So “three ways” in our Mishnah means these three and no others, which sets up the next question: what is being excluded?

Rav Sherira Gaon notes that such opening passages gather tannaitic material around seemingly trivial wording. They are neither filler nor to be over-parsed: they introduce the tractate's key vocabulary and competing models, as the opening of Bava Kamma does with *avot* and *toladot*.

sections.title: The Mishnah's Numbers: What Do 'Three' and 'Two' Exclude?
sections.gist: “Three” excludes *chuppah*, or for Rav Huna *chalipin*, which works with less than a *perutah*; “two” excludes *chalitzah*, despite a *kal va'chomer* from the *yevamah*.

bullets.text: The Mishnah counts: a woman is acquired in three ways and acquires herself in two. Each number implies that some other mode is excluded. Which?
This follows from the rule just established: “ways” marks alternatives being ruled out.

illustration.caption: The Mishnah's two counts and what each excludes (Kiddushin 3a–3b): *kesef*, *shtar* and *bi'ah* acquire her, but not *chuppah* (or, for Rav Huna, *chalipin*); a *get* or the husband's death frees her, but not *chalitzah*.

children.title: 'Three' Excludes Chuppah, or for Rav Huna, Chalipin
children.gist: The first answer is *chuppah*; since Rav Huna holds *chuppah* acquires, the number must exclude *chalipin* for him.

children.title: Chuppah Excluded, but Rav Huna Holds Chuppah Acquires
children.gist: “Three” rules out betrothal by *chuppah* alone, but Rav Huna says *chuppah* acquires, so what does the number exclude for him?

bullets.text: The number in the first clause excludes *chuppah*: it does not effect betrothal.
But Rav Huna says *chuppah* acquires, derived by a *kal va'chomer* (discussed on 5a). For him, what does the number exclude?
Rashi frames the case as a father handing his daughter over to the *chuppah*, perhaps because simply standing under a canopy is hard to picture as a legal act.

children.title: Chalipin: Ephron's Field, Less Than a Perutah, Genai or Not Kesef
children.gist: One might think *chalipin* betroths, since *kiddushin* is learned from Ephron's field, but it works with less than a *perutah*, and a woman does not give herself for that; Rashi and Tosafot explain why differently.

bullets.text: For Rav Huna the number excludes *chalipin*. One might think: betrothal is learned by *kichah kichah* from Ephron's field, and a field is acquired by *chalipin*, so a woman should be too. The Mishnah teaches otherwise.
Why not indeed? *Chalipin* works with an item worth less than a *perutah*, and a woman does not render herself acquired for less than a *perutah*.
Rashi: it would be *genai* (demeaning) to her. Using a valuable item wouldn't help: *chalipin* by nature is indifferent to value, and that character is what makes it demeaning.

Two kinds of *chalipin*: barter (my cow for your donkey), and the symbolic *kinyan* with a cloth that expresses *gemar da'at*. Barter plainly commodifies; even the symbolic kind keeps the logic of exchange.
The same object works as *kesef* when given with “*harei at mekudeshet li*”, yet fails when framed as “in exchange for this”: the framing, not the object, decides.

Tosafot: the real question was whether *chalipin* is a kind of *kesef*. Showing it works below a *perutah* proves it works through the vessel, not its value (fruit won't do), so it is not *kesef*, and only *kesef*, *shtar* and *bi'ah* betroth.
Tosafot objects to Rashi: if she consents, where is the indignity? Rashi must hold the indignity is objective, built into the transaction type.

chart.caption: Rashi and Tosafot: why *chalipin* cannot betroth a woman
rows: What acquires Ephron's field should acquire a woman
*Chalipin* works through the vessel, not its value
It isn't *kesef*, and only *kesef*, *shtar* and *bi'ah* betroth

children.title: 'Two' Excludes Chalitzah: Kal Va'chomer vs. 'Sefer Keritut'
children.gist: A *kal va'chomer* from the *yevamah* would let *chalitzah* end an ordinary marriage, but “a scroll of severance” means only a written document severs her.

bullets.text: The number in the latter clause excludes *chalitzah*.
One might argue *kal va'chomer*: a *yevamah*, whom a *get* does not release, is released by *chalitzah*. A married woman, whom a *get* does release, surely should be released by *chalitzah*.
Why not indeed? The verse says “*sefer keritut*” (Devarim 24:3): a scroll severs her from her husband, and nothing else does.

The argument is formally built but strained: *chalitzah* belongs to the specific bond of *yibum*, the man “who will not build his brother's house”. The Gemara follows the formal logic anyway and needs a verse to stop it.
Tosafot explores other *kal va'chomer* arguments that could have been raised; the Atzmot Yosef takes this further, hypothetical upon hypothetical.

chart.caption: The *kal va'chomer* for *chalitzah*, and where it breaks
rows: *Kal va'chomer*: should release her; “*sefer keritut*”: does not

sections.title: Kesef: Where It Comes From, and Why the Money Is the Father's
sections.gist: Rav derives *kiddushei kesef* from “*ein kasef*” said of the Hebrew maidservant, then defends the father's claim to the money against “let her keep it” and “at least a *na'arah* should”.

bullets.text: The Mishnah says a woman is acquired with money. From where? And Ketubot 46b says a father controls his daughter's betrothal by money, document or intercourse: from where do we know money betroths her, and that the money is his?
The Gemara starts from the father's case because in the Torah that is the primary case; a woman betrothing herself is the derived application. It is also where the *kinyan* model is most at home.
The father may betroth a minor daughter without her consent. The shiur stresses the grave moral problem when this is done through *bi'ah*, which the tradition does not paper over.

children.title: Rav: 'Ein Kasef': No Money for This Master, Money for Another
children.gist: The maidservant “goes out for nothing, without money”: her master gets nothing, which implies another master who does receive money when she leaves him, her father.

bullets.text: Rav Yehuda citing Rav: of the Hebrew maidservant, “she shall go out for nothing, *ein kasef*” (Shemot 21:11).
The extra phrase teaches: no money for this master, but there is money for another master when she leaves his authority. That master is her father.
The verse establishes that money is paid when a daughter leaves her father's domain through *kiddushin*; who keeps it is taken up next.

children.title: Why Not to Her? 'I Gave My Daughter to This Man'
children.gist: The money can't go to the daughter: the father is the one who gives her in betrothal, so it is his.

bullets.text: Challenge: perhaps the money goes to her?
Rejected: her father receives her betrothal, as it says “I gave my daughter to this man” (Devarim 22:16). Shall she take the money? Since he marries her off, the money is his.
Rashi and Tosafot note that the verse, from the case of *motzi shem ra*, speaks of a *na'arah*; it is read as a case where he betrothed her while still a minor.

children.title: Ketanah or Na'arah: 'In Her Youth, in Her Father's House'
children.gist: Perhaps the father's claim holds only for a *ketanah*, who can't receive betrothal; for a *na'arah*, who can, “in her youth, in her father's house” gives her profits to her father.

bullets.text: Challenge: perhaps this applies only to a *ketanah*, who lacks the capacity to receive her betrothal. A *na'arah* can receive it, so let her betroth herself and take the money.
Answer: “*bi'ne'ureha beit aviha*” (Bamidbar 30:17): any profit she gains in her youth belongs to her father.
The *na'arah* is the middle stage: not the *ketanah* under her father's full control, nor the *bogeret* beyond it. She has a legal “hand” of her own while her father keeps certain rights.

children.continues: Continues on 3b: Rav Huna derives a daughter's earnings from the maidservant verse instead, so “in her youth” concerns vows only; money cannot be learned from vows, fines or humiliation payments, and the Gemara returns to “*ein kasef*”.

key_terms.definition: Betrothal effected by giving the woman (or, for a minor or young woman, her father) money or an item worth at least a perutah for the sake of betrothal.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The Gemara seeks its source and why the father receives the money, deriving both from “ein kasef” said of the Hebrew maidservant.

key_terms.definition: Betrothal effected by intercourse undertaken for the sake of betrothal, one of the three modes of kiddushin listed in the Mishnah.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The Mishnah says “ways” because intercourse is called a “way”, and money and document are said to serve bi'ah as well.

key_terms.definition: A mode of acquisition in which the acquirer gives the other party an object, classically a cloth, and the property passes to him in return; the object's value does not matter.
key_terms.on_this_daf: For Rav Huna, the Mishnah's “three” excludes chalipin: though Ephron's field could be acquired this way, a woman is not, since chalipin works with less than a perutah.

key_terms.definition: The smallest coin of halakhic significance; transactions of monetary value, including betrothal by money, require at least a perutah's worth.
key_terms.on_this_daf: A woman does not give herself for less than a perutah, which rules out chalipin as a mode of betrothal.

key_terms.sense: the wedding canopy as a mode of acquisition
key_terms.definition: Bringing the bride into the husband's domain under the wedding canopy, the act that completes marriage after betrothal.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The Mishnah's “three” excludes betrothal by chuppah alone, while Rav Huna holds that chuppah does acquire.

key_terms.sense: the verbal analogy from Ephron's field
key_terms.definition: The gezeirah shavah linking the Torah's “taking” of a wife with Avraham's “taking” of Ephron's field, from which betrothal by money is learned.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The analogy suggests that chalipin, which acquires land, might betroth a woman; the Mishnah's count rejects it.

key_terms.definition: The ceremony by which a childless widow is released from the obligation to marry her late husband's brother.
key_terms.on_this_daf: A kal va'chomer from the yevamah would let chalitzah end an ordinary marriage; “sefer keritut” limits divorce to a written get.

key_terms.sense: a girl in the half year after age twelve
key_terms.definition: A girl from the onset of maturity at twelve until twelve and a half; she has legal capacity, yet remains under her father's authority for betrothal, vows and certain monies.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The Gemara asks why a na'arah, who can receive betrothal herself, doesn't keep the money, and answers from “in her youth, in her father's house”.

judgment_calls: The bi'ah answer and R. Shimon's answer are grouped under one child (s2) as the topic-based explanations of “ways”; they could instead be siblings of the zav and etrog challenges. Grouped because both explain the word from the subject of kiddushin, which the Gemara later abandons.
Zav and etrog kept in one section (s5): both are challenges answered by a natural course. They could be split into two children.

Chuppah and chalipin nested under “three” (s9), with chalitzah as a sibling under the parent question; a flat list of three exclusions would also work, but Rav Huna's chalipin answer depends on the chuppah step.
The question of 3a.4 (what the numbers exclude) is placed in the parent section's bullets instead of a separate child, since it only frames the two answers.
s7 is linked back to s2 with returns_to, since the new rule replaces those explanations; it stays where it falls in the text.

The na'arah step (s16) is the last child of the kesef-source section, though its discussion runs on past the scope; it could open a new top-level section, but the question is still about who receives the betrothal money.
coverage_notes: The shiur's opening review (nikneit vs. mekadesh, lishna d'kra, mekudeshet li, the woman as object or subject), the grammatical-gender question (shalosh), and the derekh–bi'ah link with its verse fall on 2b before this scope and are left out, apart from a clause of context in s1.
The essay says the na'arah question is left open for the next shiur; the text answers it in 3b.7 with “in her youth, in her father's house” (Bamidbar 30:17). Followed the text.

The essay presents the koy as a participant's observation about a creature the Gemara discusses elsewhere; the text raises the koy (Bikkurim 2:8) and the Gittin mishnah here, as the challenge that overturns the topic-based explanations. Followed the text; the participant's point is kept as shiur analysis.

The essay says the Gemara notes the father's authority operates against her will (al karchah); nothing in the provided text says this. Kept only as the shiur's observation about marrying off a minor, not attributed to the Gemara.
The essay does not name the author of the “ein kasef” derivation; the text gives Rav Yehuda citing Rav. Followed the text.
The essay treats “why not to her” and “I gave my daughter to this man” as separate steps; in the text the verse is the answer to the challenge. Outlined as one step.
The remainder of 3b (Rav Huna on a daughter's earnings, vows, fines and humiliation payments, 3b.8–3b.12) lies beyond this outline's scope.
